cases.note: The reason behind a crime. Prosecutors don't have to prove motive, but juries usually want to hear one.
Jack the Ripper killed at least five women in London's Whitechapel district in 1888. He was never identified.
Scotland Yard opened its fingerprint bureau in 1901. No two people, not even identical twins, share the same prints.
After the 1932 Lindbergh kidnapping, Congress made taking a victim across state lines a federal crime.
An alibi is proof a suspect was somewhere else when the crime happened. Detectives check them before they rule anyone out.
Lizzie Borden was acquitted in 1893 of killing her father and stepmother in Fall River, Massachusetts. The case was never solved.
Locard's exchange principle is usually summed up as "every contact leaves a trace." It's the idea behind most crime scene work.
Eyewitness misidentification is one of the leading causes of wrongful convictions later overturned by DNA.
The Zodiac killer taunted Northern California newspapers with ciphers. His 340-character cipher went unsolved until 2020.
Supervised release from prison before a sentence ends. Break the conditions and you can be sent back.
In 2018, a crime scene DNA sample compared through a public genealogy site led investigators to the Golden State Killer.
A serious crime, usually one that carries more than a year in prison.
In 1962, three men slipped out of Alcatraz on a raft made of raincoats. Their bodies were never found, and the FBI concluded they likely drowned.
Since a 2020 Supreme Court ruling, every state must have a unanimous jury to convict someone of a serious crime.
H.H. Holmes confessed to 27 murders, though only about nine are confirmed. Most of his crimes centered on Chicago in the 1890s, and he was hanged in Philadelphia in 1896.
Hundreds of thousands of missing-person reports are filed in the U.S. each year. Most are resolved, but thousands stay open for years.
A court's list of scheduled cases. Following a docket is how reporters track a case through the system.
Arsenic was so common in poisonings that by the 1800s it was widely known as "inheritance powder."
Miranda warnings come from a 1966 Supreme Court case, Miranda v. Arizona.
Al Capone ran Chicago's bootlegging rackets, but the government finally convicted him in 1931 for tax evasion.
Rifling inside a gun barrel leaves marks on a fired bullet that examiners can compare to a suspect's weapon.
A request for a higher court to review a conviction. Appeals look for legal errors, not new evidence.
Ground searches cover terrain in grids so no area gets skipped. Volunteers often join organized searches led by law enforcement.
Bonnie Parker and Clyde Barrow were killed in a police ambush in Bienville Parish, Louisiana, in May 1934.
Another word for detective. Thousands of amateur sleuths now help put names to unidentified remains.
The unlawful killing of another person with intent, or "malice aforethought" in legal terms.
In many rural counties, the sheriff's office, not a city police department, handles major cases.
In 1971, a man known as D.B. Cooper hijacked a Northwest flight, collected $200,000 and parachuted into the night. The FBI ended its active investigation in 2016.
A latent print is a fingerprint you can't see until it's dusted with powder, treated with chemicals or lit with special light.
To formally charge someone with a crime. The Fifth Amendment requires a grand jury indictment for serious federal crimes.
Police sketch artists build a face from a witness's memory. The hooded Unabomber sketch became one of the most recognized ever made.
The official in charge of a prison.
Corpus delicti means "body of the crime." It's proof a crime happened at all, and it doesn't have to be a body.
In 1892, the Dalton Gang tried to rob two banks at once in Coffeyville, Kansas. Townspeople fought back, and most of the gang died in the street.
K-9 teams search for missing people, and trained dogs can find a scent across fields, woods and water.
Most U.S. criminal cases never reach a jury. The large majority end with a guilty plea.
One of the three basic fingerprint patterns, with loops and arches. Loops are the most common.
The 1950 Brink's robbery in Boston took more than $2.7 million in cash and checks, the biggest robbery in U.S. history at the time.
The FBI started its Ten Most Wanted Fugitives list in 1950.
Only the president can pardon a federal crime. State crimes are pardoned by governors or state pardon boards.
Guns leave unique marks on fired cartridge casings. The ATF's NIBIN network compares them to link shootings across cities.
In 1925, Tennessee teacher John Scopes was convicted of teaching evolution and fined $100. The verdict was later overturned on a technicality.
"You have the right to remain silent" is the first line of the Miranda warning.
Missing-person flyers still matter. A photo, a last-seen location and a phone number can put a case in front of the one person who saw something.
The 1978 Lufthansa heist at New York's JFK airport took about $5 million in cash and $875,000 in jewelry.
A formal request to the judge. A motion to suppress asks the court to throw out evidence that was gathered illegally.
Dental records are one of the most reliable ways to identify unknown remains, because teeth and fillings last.
Clarence Gideon mailed a handwritten appeal to the Supreme Court. His 1963 win means anyone charged with a felony gets a lawyer, even if they can't pay.
Booking is the paperwork after an arrest: mug shot, fingerprints and a record of the charges.
Crime Stoppers programs pay rewards for tips that solve cases, and callers can stay anonymous.
To find someone not guilty. Because of double jeopardy, prosecutors can't appeal an acquittal.
In 1911, a man who had once worked at the Louvre walked out with the Mona Lisa wrapped in his work smock. It turned up in Florence two years later.
DNA can be recovered from saliva on a cup, a cigarette or the flap of an envelope, sometimes decades later.
London's Metropolitan Police, founded in 1829, is often called the first modern police force.
Habeas corpus lets a prisoner ask a court whether they're being held legally.
Mobster Bugsy Siegel helped build the Flamingo in Las Vegas. He was shot at a Beverly Hills home in 1947, and no one was ever charged.
Dive teams search lakes and rivers by touch when the water is too murky to see.
Lawyers object to stop improper questions or evidence. The judge either sustains the objection or overrules it.
Threads from clothing, carpet or a car's upholstery can tie a person or vehicle to a scene.
Bernie Madoff ran the largest Ponzi scheme in history. He was sentenced to 150 years in prison in 2009.
Cell phone records show which towers a phone connected to, which can put it, and its owner, in a general area.
To take back earlier testimony. Recanted testimony has helped overturn some wrongful convictions.
Captain William Kidd was hanged for piracy in London in 1701. Rumors of his buried treasure lasted for centuries.
Evidence bags are sealed and signed so any tampering shows. That's part of the chain of custody.
A formal accusation of a crime. Prosecutors decide what to charge, and charges can change as a case develops.
Search teams now use drones with thermal cameras to cover ground that would take volunteers days to walk.
The Teapot Dome scandal of the 1920s made Albert Fall the first Cabinet secretary sent to prison, for taking bribes.
Bloodhounds can follow a person's scent trail even after it's days old.
A judge's decision on a question of law, like whether a piece of evidence can be shown to the jury.
Jails hold people awaiting trial or serving short sentences. Prisons hold people serving longer ones.
In 1990, thieves dressed as police stole 13 works from Boston's Isabella Stewart Gardner Museum. None have been recovered.
Doorbell and business security cameras have become one of the most common sources of leads in modern cases.
Suspects can waive their Miranda rights and talk without a lawyer, and many do.
Ma Barker and her son Fred were killed during a 1935 FBI shootout at a house in Ocklawaha, Florida. Historians still argue over whether she fired a shot.
Where the dead are kept until they're identified and released to family. Many unidentified people are now listed in NamUs.
Being framed means someone planted evidence or lied to make you look guilty.
The Sixth Amendment guarantees a speedy and public trial by an impartial jury.
Dutch painter Han van Meegeren sold fake Vermeers, including one to Nazi leader Hermann Goering.
Traffic stops have caught major suspects. Timothy McVeigh was pulled over for a missing license plate about 90 minutes after the Oklahoma City bombing.
Slang for a jail or holding cell.
The 1970 RICO Act let prosecutors go after the bosses who ran criminal organizations, not just the people who did the work.
Some famous coded messages came from criminals. Two of the four Zodiac ciphers are still unsolved.
Police can briefly detain someone they reasonably suspect of a crime. That's different from an arrest.
In the Old West, an outlaw was someone placed outside the protection of the law.
A fence buys stolen goods and resells them. Tracking the fence often leads back to the thief.
